subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction:
options: Is independent of the route taken, depending only on initial and final states
questions.explain: Because enthalpy is a state function, alternative routes give the same overall ΔH.

questions.q: Hess's law is useful because it allows enthalpy changes to be found:
options: Indirectly, when they cannot be measured experimentally
questions.explain: Enthalpy cycles let us calculate ΔH for reactions that are hard to carry out directly.

questions.q: Using bond enthalpies, ΔH of a reaction is calculated as:
questions.explain: ΔH = Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds formed).

questions.q: Bond enthalpy calculations give only approximate ΔH values because:
options: Bond enthalpies are average values across many compounds
They only apply to ionic compounds
Bonds have exact fixed energies in all molecules
questions.explain: Average bond enthalpies vary slightly with molecular environment, so results are approximate.

questions.q: The standard enthalpy change of formation is the enthalpy change when:
options: One mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states
One mole of gas is heated
questions.explain: By definition the ΔHf of an element in its standard state is zero.

questions.q: Entropy (S) is a measure of the:
options: Disorder or number of ways energy and matter can be arranged
questions.explain: Greater disorder (more microstates) corresponds to higher entropy.

questions.q: Which change is expected to have a positive entropy change (ΔS > 0)?
options: Two gases combining into fewer gas molecules
questions.explain: Forming a gas from a solid greatly increases disorder, so ΔS is positive.

questions.q: The Gibbs free energy change is given by:
questions.explain: T is the absolute temperature in kelvin.

questions.q: A reaction is spontaneous (feasible) when:
questions.explain: A negative Gibbs free energy change indicates a thermodynamically spontaneous reaction.

questions.q: For a reaction with ΔH negative and ΔS positive, the reaction is:
questions.explain: With ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative at every temperature.

questions.q: For a reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS positive, it becomes spontaneous:
questions.explain: When TΔS exceeds ΔH, ΔG becomes negative, so high temperature favours spontaneity.

questions.q: At the temperature where a reaction is at equilibrium between spontaneous and non-spontaneous, ΔG equals:
questions.explain: At ΔG = 0 the system is at the boundary of spontaneity (e.g. a phase change at its transition temperature).

questions.q: If ΔHf values are known for all reactants and products, ΔH of reaction equals:
options: Sum of ΔHf(products) minus sum of ΔHf(reactants)
questions.explain: This Hess's law relationship uses standard enthalpies of formation.

questions.q: Melting ice into liquid water has a ΔS that is:
options: Positive, as the liquid is more disordered than the solid
questions.explain: Liquid water has more freedom of arrangement than the ordered solid lattice.

questions.q: Enthalpy is described as a state function, which means it:
options: Depends only on the current state, not the path taken
questions.explain: This is the basis of Hess's law.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +50 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100 J/K/mol. At 298 K, TΔS is about 29.8 kJ/mol, so ΔG is:
options: Positive (about +20 kJ/mol), so non-spontaneous at this temperature
questions.explain: ΔG = 50 − 29.8 = +20.2 kJ/mol; the reaction would need a higher temperature to become spontaneous.

questions.q: Dissolving an ionic solid that increases disorder in solution generally has:
questions.explain: Dispersing ions into solution usually increases disorder, giving positive ΔS.

questions.q: An energy cycle that relates lattice enthalpy to formation and other enthalpy terms is a:
questions.explain: A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to ionic compound formation.

questions.q: A reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS negative is:
questions.explain: With ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0, ΔG is always positive.

questions.q: Given a two-step route with ΔH1 = -200 kJ and ΔH2 = +50 kJ, the overall ΔH by Hess's law is:
questions.explain: Overall ΔH = ΔH1 + ΔH2 = -200 + 50 = -150 kJ.
